title: One Coffee House in a Run-Down Nairobi Arcade: Java's 1999 Start
dek: In 1999 former relief workers opened a single coffee house on Ngong Road, in a country that exported nearly all its coffee and had no café habit.

story.event: Opening a single coffee house at Adams Arcade on Ngong Road
story.summary: In 1999 Kevin Ashley, Jon Wagner and fellow American former relief workers opened Nairobi Java House at Adams Arcade on Ngong Road, when Kenya had almost no café culture and its economy was struggling. They learned to roast in the United States, bought equipment from Dubai and planned only one coffee house; the chain grew slowly from its own revenues, taking ten years to reach ten branches, before a majority stake was sold to Emerging Capital Partners in 2012.
paragraphs: In 1999 Kevin Ashley and a few fellow American former relief workers opened a coffee house in Adams Arcade, a run-down shopping centre on Ngong Road in Nairobi. Ashley had first come to Africa as a 22-year-old backpacker and later spent years on relief work in southern Sudan. There, he recalled, he and colleagues would drive to Kakuma refugee camp to buy green beans from Ethiopian traders, roast them in frying pans and pound them by hand. It was better, he said, than any coffee in the shops.

What they knew argued against the idea. Kenya's economy was struggling and there were no modern malls. Kenyans drank tea: for decades nearly all the coffee had been exported, and farmers had been barred from roasting beans for local sale. Nairobi had no proper coffee shops. "People thought we were crazy to try to sell coffee to Kenyans," his co-founder Jon Wagner told The Guardian in 2007. Ashley said they wanted something more stable than the aviation business he had co-founded, flying aircraft in war zones.

They kept the plan small. They went to the United States to learn to roast, bought equipment from Dubai, and learned to roast and bake in a shared kitchen. The idea, Ashley said, was simply that Nairobi needed a good coffee house and somewhere to have breakfast; nobody planned more branches. At first about two-thirds of customers were expatriates and affluent Asians, and waiters favoured foreigners' tables in hope of bigger tips, so staff had to be trained to serve everyone equally. The first three to five years were, he said, "really tough", with partners split over whether to sell alcohol or stay a family place.

Growth was slow and paid for out of takings. By 2007 there were seven outlets and more than 70 per cent of customers were Kenyan. It took ten years to reach ten branches. In 2012, with 13 branches and annual turnover near Sh1 billion, a majority stake was sold to the private equity firm Emerging Capital Partners. Asked in 2015 to pick a favourite branch, Ashley chose Adams Arcade because it was where they started, and said it showed how "young and stupid" they had been.

quote.text: I settle myself ever the firmer in the creed that we should not postpone and refer and wish, but do broad justice where we are, by whomsoever we deal with
quote.source_title: Essays — Second Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2945
quote.connection: Emerson's creed was to stop postponing and do justice where you stand, to whoever is in front of you. Java began as one modest room rather than a plan for a chain, and one of its first lessons was a waiter's: every table, foreign or Kenyan, was owed the same service.

reflection: Ashley and his partners did not set out to build East Africa's largest coffee chain. They set out to make one good place: coffee they wanted to drink, breakfast, a room people would come back to. The chain came later and slowly, paid for out of takings, after years he called tough.

When you are building something, it is easy to live in the future version of it. Emerson's advice is to do broad justice where you are. Today that might mean giving your whole attention to the one person or piece of work in front of you, and letting the larger plan wait its turn.
invitation: Before you open your plans for the week, choose one person you will work with or serve today, and give that conversation your full attention, as if it were the only branch you had.

research_notes: Founders: Ashley told Business Daily (2015) that he founded Java 'together with three others'; How we made it in Africa (2014) says three US-born former relief workers; Business Daily (2012), The Kenya Times and The Guardian name Kevin Ashley and Jon (John) Wagner. The story names Ashley and Wagner and refers to 'a few fellow American former relief workers' without a number. The slate named Ashley alone; Wagner is added because he is named co-founder in three sources and is the co-founder quoted on how the idea was first received. Branch counts: The Guardian gives seven outlets in 2007; Business Daily (2015) says ten branches from 1999 to 2010 and How we made it in Africa quotes Ashley 'It took us 10 years to grow to 10 branches'; Business Daily (2012) gives 13 branches in May 2012. These are consistent and the story uses each with its year. Turnover: 'touching Sh1 billion' for the year to June 2011 is Ashley's figure as reported by Business Daily (2012). Ashley's Sudan years: How we made it in Africa says five years of relief work in South Sudan; Business Daily and Africa Outlook place him at Lokichoggio and the Kenya-Sudan border with the World Food Programme from 1993; the story says 'years on relief work in southern Sudan'. Funding is recorded as bootstrapped: Business Daily (2012) says expansion had been funded from internal revenues until the ECP deal. Africa Outlook's text partly repeats Ashley's Business Daily answers, so it is used only alongside, not as an independent confirmation of his own memories. The Emerson line is from the essay's closing reflections on living in the present.
